changes.before: The fake captured one message. Which conclusion is supported?
changes.after: A fake service can test how your code uses it. It cannot prove the real service worked.

before: A test double replaces a dependency with controlled behavior. It can isolate the code you are testing, but it cannot establish that the real dependency behaves the same way.
A fake mailer records a message in an array. A passing test can show that your function requested the right recipient and text. It cannot prove a real email was delivered.

send is a method on the fake object. push appends the supplied message to an in-memory array. length counts captured requests. There is no network operation, delivery receipt, inbox check, or production credential here.
Changed situation: The fake captured one message. Which conclusion is supported?
The evidence covers the fake interaction. A real integration requires separate, authorized verification.
after: A test double is a controlled replacement for something your code uses. It helps you test one part without relying on a real service.
A fake mailer can store requested messages in an array. Then a test can inspect their recipients and text.
send is a method: a function stored on the mailer object. push adds the message to sent. length counts the captured requests.
The result proves that this fake received one message. It does not show that any email reached an inbox.
A real delivery check needs a separate test using an intended test recipient and the real service. Keep that claim separate from the fake's result.
